$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{5}x+2y)=2\sqrt{5}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{5}x+2y)=2,\end{aligned}

$$

$$
z=2y+{x}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 8x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d2/d2ca6ee66367bd86cd56fe3a4891dbd4b64d9e23d5b4d97c9650b3af184b423f.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+{x}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+{x}^{2})=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{8x}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8x\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 5 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2bc578f-8afe-5a87-8c83-39f18d34c660"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b2bc578f-8afe-5a87-8c83-39f18d34c660" :answer-field/id #uuid "b2bc578f-8afe-5a87-8c83-39f18d34c660" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-cf2a1588-1e59-59e9-802e-6ebad0b0fea0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c4b6f195-b9dc-56ca-a43b-6af6cf36c33b" "answer-b4f9a248-c377-505f-ac3a-9e96059ce3f5" "answer-cf2a1588-1e59-59e9-802e-6ebad0b0fea0" "answer-3dc37952-1697-5509-8bc7-6ccd85ec6880" "answer-aea19d27-cea1-5633-a35f-860030bc1eeb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4b6f195-b9dc-56ca-a43b-6af6cf36c33b" :answer/id #uuid "c4b6f195-b9dc-56ca-a43b-6af6cf36c33b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi \sqrt{17}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b4f9a248-c377-505f-ac3a-9e96059ce3f5" :answer/id #uuid "b4f9a248-c377-505f-ac3a-9e96059ce3f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\pi (\sqrt{17}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf2a1588-1e59-59e9-802e-6ebad0b0fea0" :answer/id #uuid "cf2a1588-1e59-59e9-802e-6ebad0b0fea0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi \sqrt{14}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3dc37952-1697-5509-8bc7-6ccd85ec6880" :answer/id #uuid "3dc37952-1697-5509-8bc7-6ccd85ec6880" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6\pi \sqrt{14}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aea19d27-cea1-5633-a35f-860030bc1eeb" :answer/id #uuid "aea19d27-cea1-5633-a35f-860030bc1eeb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi (\sqrt{14}-2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176989 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Now, if our surface $S$ is defined as $z= f(x,y),$ then it can always be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf r(x,y)= \left\langle x,\: y,\: f(x,y)\right\rangle  \qquad (x,y)  \in D.
$$

In this case, the variables $x$ and $y$ act as parameters. 

Thus, the fundamental vector product of $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂f}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨-\frac{∂f}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂f}{∂y},\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and using the fact that $z = f(x,y),$ we can write this as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨-\frac{∂z}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂z}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| = \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}.
$$

So, we conclude that for a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Let's look at an example of how to apply this formula." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176990 :tutorial/content "![](images/86/867722106ffd8445b62a98ab43197ac2fba646faff95017ef7e92c254a97fb6e.png)

  

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2, \quad (x,y) \in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176142 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Now, if our surface $S$ is defined as $z= f(x,y),$ then it can always be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf r(x,y)= \left\langle x,\: y,\: f(x,y)\right\rangle  \qquad (x,y)  \in D.
$$

In this case, the variables $x$ and $y$ act as parameters. 

Thus, the fundamental vector product of $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂f}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨-\frac{∂f}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂f}{∂y},\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and using the fact that $z = f(x,y),$ we can write this as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨-\frac{∂z}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂z}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| = \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}.
$$

So, we conclude that for a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2, \quad (x,y) \in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f3795a6-1971-55b3-9109-8565cd3830a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5344 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "20aafc3a-c734-59a5-9792-c59b83342b12" :step/math-academy-id 33441 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176721}} {:db/id 17592186176747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186175996 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175848 :question/id #uuid "77e8fb3e-1858-5831-b740-a0c133c8180f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9141"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8c0f4b8-0b77-5e8a-aae2-2d27ea125d82" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049997}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176212} {:db/id 17592186176243} {:db/id 17592186278397} {:db/id 17592186278398} {:db/id 17592186278400} {:db/id 17592186278413} {:db/id 17592186389160} {:db/id 17592186389167}] :knowledge-point/title "Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains"} :step/id #uuid "dd0b86de-1ce8-5231-a10e-a2cb302f264c" :step/math-academy-id 34075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176887}} {:db/id 17592186176884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176065 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175710 :question/id #uuid "7498df7d-a340-599e-b4ba-496f5142c28c" :question/math-academy-id "e-12379"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2966982a-a726-53e7-923f-2ca43760b756" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176248} {:db/id 17592186176395} {:db/id 17592186278404} {:db/id 17592186278405} {:db/id 17592186278406} {:db/id 17592186278407} {:db/id 17592186278408} {:db/id 17592186278409}] :knowledge-point/title "Changing to Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "95a582e7-cf2f-5cb4-a271-ae31cf32d50a" :step/math-academy-id 44417} {:db/id 17592186176887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177075 :tutorial/content "We have similar formulas for the areas of surfaces defined by $x = f(y,z)$ and $y = f(x,z){:}$

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2, \quad (x,y) \in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f3795a6-1971-55b3-9109-8565cd3830a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5344 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186176887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177075 :tutorial/content "We have similar formulas for the areas of surfaces defined by $x = f(y,z)$ and $y = f(x,z){:}$

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $yz$-plane.

- For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by
